title: Navigation and deep links
summary: Stack, tab and drawer navigators, typed route params, the back stack, and how deep links map URLs to screens.

sections.title: There is no URL bar
sections.body: Mobile apps have no built-in router. A navigation library keeps a state object: a stack of routes, each with a `name`, a unique `key` and `params`. Navigators render it: a stack shows the top route with push and pop animations, tabs keep one route per tab alive, and drawers slide in a menu. Navigators nest, so a tab can hold its own stack.

sections.title: Moving around
sections.body:
The common actions on a stack:

- `navigate(name, params)`: go to the route, reusing an existing one with that name if it is already in the stack.
- `push(name, params)`: always add a new route on top, even if one with that name exists.
- `goBack()` / `pop()`: remove the top route. On Android the hardware back button does this.
- `popToTop()`: back to the first route.
- `replace(name, params)`: swap the top route, so back skips it (useful after login).
- `reset(state)`: replace the whole state, for example after logout.
sections.code:
type RootStack = { Home: undefined; Product: { id: string }; Cart: undefined }

navigation.navigate('Product', { id: '42' })
navigation.push('Product', { id: '43' }) // two Product screens in the stack
navigation.replace('Cart')

sections.title: Params and types
sections.body: Params must be serialisable: ids and simple values, not functions or whole objects. Pass the id and load the data on the screen, so a deep link and an in-app tap produce the same screen. Type the param list once and the navigator checks every `navigate` call.

sections.title: Deep links
sections.body:
A deep link opens the app at a screen: `shop://product/42` or a verified https universal or app link. You map path patterns to screens, such as `product/:id`, and the library parses the URL into a navigation state with params. Query strings become extra params. Unknown paths should fall back to a sensible screen.

Cold start (app launched by the link) and warm start (app already running) arrive through different callbacks, so handle both.

Exercises here run as TypeScript in a browser sandbox with no React Native runtime, so they model this logic as plain functions and reducers. The same functions drop straight into a real app: call them from a component, a hook or a store.

pitfalls: Passing non-serialisable params such as callbacks, which breaks state persistence and deep links.
Using `navigate` when you need a second instance of the same screen; use `push`.
Not handling the Android back button in custom flows such as modals.
Only handling deep links on warm start.

gotchas.question: The stack is `Home > Product(1)`. What does `navigate('Product', { id: '2' })` do by default?
gotchas.answer: It goes to the existing `Product` route and updates its params rather than pushing a second one. `push` would add a new route on top.

gotchas.question: After login you call `replace('Home')` on the stack `Login`. What happens when the user presses back?
gotchas.answer: The app exits or goes to the previous navigator, because `Login` was replaced and is no longer in the stack.

gotchas.question: How should `shop://product/42?ref=email` reach the screen?
gotchas.answer: Map `product/:id` to the `Product` screen. The params become `{ id: '42', ref: 'email' }`; path params and query params are merged.
